text: Grey, sweaty, mottled, agitated or drowsy.
Central cyanosis: a blue tongue and lips.
Lying very still, afraid to move; or writhing and unable to settle.
Tachycardia: above 100 /min.
Bradycardia: below 60 /min.
Irregularly irregular.
Hypotension: systolic below 90 mmHg or mean pressure below 65 mmHg.
Wide pulse pressure with a low diastolic.
Narrow pulse pressure.
Tachypnoea: above 20 /min.
Bradypnoea: below 10 /min.
Below 94 % on room air.
Fever: 38.0 °C or more.
Hypothermia: below 36 °C in an unwell patient, or below 35 °C.
note: Threshold differs from the sign definition; decide.

text: Irregularly irregular.
Collapsing (water-hammer) pulse: a sharp rise and a quick fall, felt best with the arm raised.
Weak and fast (thready).
Slow-rising, small-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).
Bounding, collapsing pulse; or a double peak (bisferiens).
Raised JVP.
JVP not visible even with the patient flat.
Cannon waves: large irregular a waves.
Displaced down and out, diffuse.
Not displaced but sustained and heaving.
A harsh ejection systolic (crescendo–decrescendo) murmur radiating to the carotids; a soft or absent S2.
A loud pulmonary component of S2.
A wide split of S2 that does not change with breathing (fixed splitting).
note: No condition linked (atrial septal defect has no diagnosis id).

text: A soft, high-pitched early diastolic murmur, decrescendo.
An ejection systolic murmur that gets louder on standing or straining.
A pansystolic murmur that gets louder on inspiration.
A scratchy, superficial sound with up to three components, varying with position.
A pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.
A third heart sound (gallop) early in diastole.
A fourth heart sound just before S1.
A low-pitched, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur, often after an opening snap.
note: The card links aortic regurgitation (Austin Flint); an opening snap belongs to mitral stenosis, which has no diagnosis id. Review.

text: A third or fourth heart sound.
A soft, blowing, high-pitched early diastolic murmur.
A scratchy rub.
A bruit loudest high in the neck.
A murmur loudest at the base of the neck and louder still over the aortic area.
note: A transmitted murmur, not a bruit.

text: Bronchial breathing: harsh, expiration as long and loud as inspiration, with a gap between.
Reduced or absent breath sounds.
Wheeze: musical, mainly expiratory, often from many airways at once.
Fine end-inspiratory crackles at the bases.
Coarse crackles that may change with coughing.
A creaking pleural rub.
Stony dull.
Dull.
Hyper-resonant.
Increased: the words come through clearly, even when whispered.
Reduced or absent.

text: Prolonged expiration through pursed lips.
Deep, sighing breaths at a normal or raised rate (Kussmaul).
note: Kussmaul breathing: deep breathing caused by a metabolic acidosis.

text: Waxing and waning breathing with pauses (Cheyne–Stokes).
Deviated away from the abnormal side.
note: Qualifier: away.

text: Deviated towards the abnormal side.
note: Qualifier: towards.

text: Reduced on one side.
note: Qualifier: one side.

text: Reduced on both sides.
note: Qualifier: both sides.

text: The saturation hardly rises despite a high inspired fraction.
The saturation rises easily.
note: A response, not a sign: hypoxaemia that corrects (qualifier oxygen-responsive).

note: CO₂ narcosis: consciousness is not an observable yet.

text: Refill slower than the normal limit for age and sex, in a warm room.
Bilateral pitting oedema.
One swollen, warm, tender calf.
Non-pitting swelling.
Yellow sclerae.
The front rim is as pale as the rest (no rim contrast).
The hands drop forward briefly and jerk back, irregularly, on both sides.
Dullness that shifts when the patient turns.
Black, sticky, tarry stool with a characteristic smell (melaena).
A hard, irregular mass in the rectum; fresh blood.
Lax anal tone and reduced perianal sensation.
A smoothly enlarged prostate.
Several spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, leukonychia.
Caput medusae.
A fine, fast tremor of the outstretched fingers.
Dark palmar creases, brown patches inside the cheeks, pigmented scars.
A diffuse, smooth, soft goitre with a bruit.
An irregular, nodular goitre.
A tender gland, often after a viral illness.
Lid retraction and lid lag.
Proptosis, chemosis, restricted eye movements, double vision.
note: Restrictive ophthalmopathy is not modelled; double vision is a symptom.

text: A dry tongue and dry mucosa.
A smooth, red, sore tongue (glossitis); cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis).
The fold stays up and flattens slowly (tenting).
Sweet, fruity, like pear drops or nail-varnish remover.
Musty, sweetish (fetor hepaticus).
Ammonia-like, fishy (uraemic fetor).
Heart rate rises by 30 /min or more, or standing is impossible because of dizziness.
Systolic falls by 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic by 10 or more, within 3 minutes.
Guarding, rigidity, rebound or percussion tenderness.
Tenderness in the right iliac fossa.
Epigastric tenderness.
Enlarged spleen, with or without the liver.
A smooth, dull mass rising from the pelvis that cannot be got below.
Loin tenderness, worse on gentle punching.
A small pupil with a slight drooping of the same lid.
A large pupil with a complete ptosis, the eye turned down and out.
Nystagmus while looking straight ahead.
The difference grows in the dark, the small pupil widening slowly.
The difference is greater in bright light.
note: Qualifier: greater in light (the large pupil is abnormal).

text: One pupil does not constrict, whichever eye is lit.
Light in one eye constricts neither pupil; light in the other constricts both.
note: Qualifier: absolute (amaurotic).

text: Both pupils widen when the light swings to one eye.
One eye fails to abduct, with horizontal double vision.
The eye is down and out, with ptosis.
Horizontal nystagmus beating in one direction, stronger when looking that way.
Nystagmus that changes direction with the direction of gaze; jerky pursuit.
Double vision that varies and worsens with effort.
Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating in one direction, much stronger without fixation.
Purely vertical or purely torsional nystagmus, or nystagmus no stronger without fixation.
A catch-up saccade after turning towards one side.
A normal head impulse in a patient with acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus.
note: A pertinent negative: the absence of head-impulse-positive within the pattern.

text: A vertical refixation: one eye moves down, the other up.
A horizontal refixation.
The same half of the field lost in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia).
The outer halves lost in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopia).
A central blind spot in one eye (central scotoma).
A swollen disc with blurred margins, lost venous pulsation, haemorrhages around it.
A pale disc.
Cannot repeat the whisper on one side.
Bone conduction louder than air (Rinne negative).
Louder in the deaf ear.
Louder in the better ear.
Steady with the eyes open, but sways and falls when they close (Romberg positive).
Falls consistently towards one side when the eyes close.
Unsteady even with the eyes open, feet together impossible.
Broad-based, staggering; cannot walk heel to toe.
Veers to one side but walks unaided.
One leg stiff and swung outwards in a semicircle, the arm flexed.
High stepping, the foot slapping down.
Stamping, watching the feet, worse in the dark.
A tremor that grows near the target, and overshooting (past-pointing), with eyes open as much as closed.
Accurate with eyes open, lost with eyes closed.
Weakness of the whole of one side, forehead included; the eye does not close.
Weakness of the lower face with the forehead spared.
Weakness on both sides.
Loss on one side of the face together with the body on the same side.
Loss of pain on one side of the face and on the opposite side of the body.
An absent corneal reflex on one side.
The jaw deviates to one side on opening.
A brisk jaw jerk.
The uvula is pulled to one side.
The palate hardly moves on either side; nasal speech.
note: Palatal movement itself is not modelled.

text: Deviates to one side when stuck out, with wasting on that side.
Wasted, fasciculating tongue.
Deviates slightly towards the weak side of the body, without wasting.
Weak shrug or head turning on one side, with wasting.
note: Wasting of trapezius is not modelled.

text: Weak neck and shoulders on both sides.
note: Qualifier: both sides.

text: Halting, effortful speech with good comprehension (expressive aphasia).
Fluent speech full of wrong words, with poor comprehension (receptive aphasia).
Slurred, scanning or explosive speech with normal language.
The voice becomes quieter, nasal and slurred as the count goes on.
Running out of breath early.
One or both lids sink progressively.
A catch that gives way, worse with faster movement (spasticity).
Even resistance throughout (lead-pipe), or ratchet-like (cogwheel).
Floppy with wasting and fasciculation.
Extensors weaker than flexors (pyramidal pattern), on one side.
Weakness confined to the muscles of one root (myotome).
Symmetrical weakness, proximal or ascending.
Weakness with wasting and fasciculation, mixed with brisk reflexes.
note: Mixed UMN and LMN signs: motor neurone disease.

text: Brisk, spreading reflexes on one side.
Reflexes absent even with reinforcement.
Loss in one dermatome.
Loss over a whole half of the body, face included.
Loss in the body on one side and the face on the other.
Vibration and position sense lost at the fingertips.
Spastic tone; sustained clonus.
Floppy, wasted leg.
Weak dorsiflexion and big toe extension, with weak inversion.
note: Qualifier: inversion weak (L5).

text: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with normal inversion.
note: Qualifier: inversion spared (peroneal).

text: Weak plantarflexion and eversion.
note: S1 myotome.

text: Flexors weaker than extensors, on one side, with the arm.
Symmetrical weakness rising from the feet.
The big toe extends upwards and the other toes fan (Babinski sign).
Absent ankle reflex on one side.
All reflexes absent.
Absent ankle reflexes with upgoing plantars.
note: Mixed pattern: B12 deficiency, motor neurone disease.

text: Loss on the top of the foot and big toe.
note: L5 or the superficial peroneal nerve.

text: Loss on the outer foot and sole.
Loss in both feet, fading upwards (stocking).
Vibration and position sense lost at the toes.
Strength fades with repetition and recovers with rest.
One arm turns palm-down and sinks.
One arm rises or wanders, the fingers moving restlessly.
Pain shooting down the leg below the knee between 30° and 70°.
The heel overshoots or misses the knee (dysmetria) and wobbles off the shin; the tremor grows as it nears the target (intention tremor), with the eyes open as much as closed.
Accurate while the patient watches, but the heel wanders once the eyes are closed.
The leg cannot be lifted onto the knee, or only slowly and with effort.
note: Weakness limits the test; not ataxia.

text: Slow, irregular and clumsy, the rhythm breaking down (dysdiadochokinesis).
Slow but regular.
A level below which pinprick is reduced.
Reduced perianal sensation, often with urinary retention and lax anal tone.
Breathless lying flat, better sitting up (orthopnoea).
The JVP is visible at the angle of the jaw at 45°.
Insists on sitting bolt upright, leaning on the arms (tripod).
Chest pain eased by sitting forward.
note: A symptom, not a sign: belongs in the history (pericarditis).

text: A diastolic rumble or third heart sound heard only in this position.
Dizzy or faint on standing.
note: A symptom; the sign is orthostatic-hypotension or postural-tachycardia.

text: A systolic murmur that gets louder on standing.
A midline sternotomy scar, a thoracotomy scar, a pacemaker under the clavicle.
A barrel-shaped chest.
A distended abdomen with full flanks and an everted umbilicus.
An abdomen that does not move with breathing.
